title: Unit 12: Quant Corner
subtitle: Probability, data, and the math of markets

questions.prompt: What does 'expected value' (EV) mean?
choices: The long-run average outcome, found by adding each outcome times its probability
The result you personally hope will happen
The single biggest amount you could win
A payout you are guaranteed to receive
questions.explanation: EV is the probability-weighted average of every outcome, so it tells you what a bet is worth over many tries, not on any one try.

questions.prompt: A game gives a 30% chance to win $10 and a 70% chance to win nothing. What is its expected value, in dollars?
questions.explanation: (0.30 x $10) + (0.70 x $0) = $3. On average each play is worth $3, even though most plays win $0.

questions.prompt: A bet can have positive expected value and still lose on any single try.
questions.explanation: Positive EV means it pays off on average over many tries, but luck still decides a single outcome.

questions.prompt: Why do casinos reliably make money over time?
choices: Every game is tilted slightly in the house's favor, and that tiny edge repeats over millions of bets
They cheat at every single table
Players always run out of luck at midnight
They don't actually profit; casinos usually lose
questions.explanation: A small 'house edge' per bet, multiplied by a huge number of bets, turns into steady profit. Edge plus repetition wins.

questions.prompt: Sort each bet into positive or negative expected value.
items: A lottery that returns 60 cents on average per $1 ticket
questions.explanation: Compare the average payout to the cost: $1 for a $2.50 average is positive, but $2 for a $1.50 average is negative. Most lottery tickets are negative EV.

questions.prompt: Which statements about expected value are true? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: It weights each outcome by how likely it is
A positive-EV bet can still lose on a single try
It promises you a profit every single time
Negative-EV bets tend to lose money if repeated many times
questions.explanation: EV is a long-run average, not a guarantee. Positive EV wins over many tries; negative EV bleeds money over many tries.

questions.prompt: The house edge is the reason that, over enough spins, the casino comes out ahead of the player.
questions.explanation: Each game keeps a little more than it pays back, so the more you play, the more that edge grows in the house's favor.

questions.prompt: What is 'backtesting'?
choices: Checking how a strategy would have performed on historical data before risking real money
Testing your posture while you trade
Selling stocks you bought last week
Reviewing your monthly bank statement
questions.explanation: Quants replay history to ask 'would this rule have worked?' It is a cheap way to throw out bad ideas before betting real cash.

questions.prompt: A strategy that made money in the past is guaranteed to make money in the future.
questions.explanation: Markets change and patterns fade once everyone spots them. Past performance never guarantees future results.

questions.prompt: Your friend's one stock pick doubled. What would a quant say about copying them?
choices: One result is far too small a sample; luck and skill look identical after a single trade
One win proves they are a genius
Always copy whoever won most recently
Sample size never matters
questions.explanation: Flip enough coins and someone gets five heads in a row. You need many results to tell real skill from a lucky streak.

questions.prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise every summer. What does this show?
choices: Correlation isn't causation; a third factor (hot, sunny weather) drives both
Ice cream causes sunburn
Sunburn makes people crave ice cream
The data must be wrong
questions.explanation: Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. A hidden third cause is a classic trap in market data too.

questions.prompt: Match each data idea to its meaning.
pairs: Testing a rule on past data
How many data points you have
A rule tuned so tightly to old data it fails on new data
questions.explanation: These four ideas are the backbone of thinking with data instead of gut feelings.

questions.prompt: You flip a fair coin 10 times. How many heads would you EXPECT on average? (Whole number.)
questions.explanation: Expected heads = 10 flips x 50% = 5. Any single run of 10 flips can differ, but 5 is the long-run average.

questions.prompt: Order these sample sizes from LEAST to MOST trustworthy for spotting a real pattern.
questions.explanation: The bigger the sample, the more luck averages out and the clearer any real pattern becomes.

questions.prompt: What is a 'trend' on a price chart?
choices: The general direction prices are moving over time: up, down, or sideways
The exact price at this second
A guarantee of tomorrow's price
The number of shares traded today
questions.explanation: A trend is the overall drift of prices across many days, not any single day's move.

questions.prompt: What is a 'moving average'?
choices: The average price over a recent window that slides forward, smoothing out day-to-day jumps
The fastest price change of the day
The all-time highest price of a stock
A fee charged for each trade
questions.explanation: It averages the last few prices and updates each day, drawing a smoother line that makes the trend easier to see.

questions.prompt: A moving average smooths out short-term noise to make the underlying trend easier to see.
questions.explanation: By averaging recent prices, it flattens random wiggles so the bigger direction stands out.

questions.prompt: The last 3 closing prices were $8, $10, and $12. What is the 3-day moving average, in dollars?
questions.explanation: ($8 + $10 + $12) / 3 = $30 / 3 = $10. You add the recent prices and divide by how many there are.

questions.prompt: Match each chart term to what it means.
pairs: A smoothed line of recent prices
questions.explanation: Reading charts is mostly about separating the signal (the trend) from the noise (the random jitter).

questions.prompt: Order these time frames from shortest to longest.
questions.explanation: Zooming out from minutes to months is how analysts tell short-term noise apart from the long-term trend.

questions.prompt: Which statements about reading charts are true? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: A moving average lags a bit because it is built from past prices
Short-term price wiggles are often just noise
A chart pattern guarantees what happens next
Longer time frames help reveal the bigger trend
questions.explanation: Charts describe the past and hint at direction, but no pattern can promise the future.

questions.prompt: Why should you never put all your money into one trade?
choices: A single loss could wipe you out, and you can't recover from zero
One trade is always illegal
It makes your taxes higher
Brokers ban large trades
questions.explanation: If everything rides on one bet and it fails, you have nothing left to bounce back with. Surviving losses is rule one.

questions.prompt: What is diversification?
choices: Spreading money across many different investments so one loss can't sink you
Buying as much of one hot stock as possible
Keeping all your cash under a mattress
Trading only on Fridays
questions.explanation: When your money is spread out, a single bad investment is only a small dent, not a disaster.

questions.prompt: Position sizing means deciding how much money to put into a single trade.
questions.explanation: Choosing the size of each bet is how you control how much a loss can hurt you.

questions.prompt: You have $1,000 and follow a rule to risk at most 2% on any single trade. What is the most you'd risk, in dollars?
questions.explanation: 2% of $1,000 = $20. Keeping each risk tiny means a losing streak can't blow up your whole account.

questions.prompt: After a 50% loss, you need a 100% gain just to get back to where you started.
questions.explanation: Drop from $100 to $50, and you must double that $50 back to $100, which is a 100% gain. Losses hurt more than they look.

questions.prompt: Sort each action into whether it manages or increases your risk.
items: Putting your entire savings into one stock
Risking only a small percent per trade
Keeping some cash on the sidelines
questions.explanation: Diversifying, sizing small, and holding cash cushion you; concentrating everything or using borrowed money amplifies the danger.

questions.prompt: Which are smart risk and position-sizing rules? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Never put all your money in one bet
Diversify across different investments
Size trades so a losing streak won't ruin you
Bet bigger after every loss to win it back
questions.explanation: Doubling down to chase losses is how people blow up accounts. Staying diversified and sized to survive is the pro move.

questions.prompt: What is a 'quant'?
choices: Someone who uses math, statistics, and code to find and trade patterns in markets
A person who only trades gold coins
A banker who never touches computers
A news reporter who covers stocks
questions.explanation: Short for 'quantitative analyst', a quant turns market ideas into numbers, models, and code.

questions.prompt: What is high-frequency trading (HFT)?
choices: Computers making huge numbers of trades in fractions of a second
Trading once a year on your birthday
Buying a stock and holding it for decades
Trading only during lunch
questions.explanation: HFT firms use fast computers and code to place enormous numbers of tiny, split-second trades.

questions.prompt: Math and models can reduce and manage risk, but they can never delete it completely.
questions.explanation: Even the best model is a simplification of a messy world, so surprises still happen. Risk is managed, never erased.

questions.prompt: Order how a quant typically builds a strategy.
items: Form an idea about the market
Turn it into a testable rule
Risk a small amount of real money
questions.explanation: Idea, rule, backtest, then a small live test: that careful loop is how quants avoid betting big on a hunch.

questions.prompt: Match each quant tool or term to what it does.
pairs: A set of rules a computer follows to trade
Checking a strategy against past data
A math simplification of how something works
questions.explanation: Quants combine these tools to test ideas and control risk instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: What do quants actually rely on? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Probability and statistics
Computer code and algorithms
A crystal ball that predicts prices perfectly
Careful risk management
questions.explanation: Quants lean on math, code, and risk control. Nobody, quant or not, can predict prices perfectly.

questions.prompt: Because models can be wrong, quants still use risk limits and position sizing to survive surprises.
questions.explanation: Smart quants assume they'll be wrong sometimes, so they size bets to live through the losses.

questions.prompt: Which best defines expected value?
choices: The probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes
The most money you could possibly win
The result you are hoping for
A guaranteed profit
questions.explanation: EV weights each outcome by its odds, giving the long-run average of a bet, not a promise about any single try.

questions.prompt: A bet has a 40% chance to win $20 and a 60% chance to win nothing. What is its expected value, in dollars?
questions.explanation: (0.40 x $20) + (0.60 x $0) = $8. That's the average value per play over many tries.

questions.prompt: If two things are correlated, it proves that one of them causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation; a hidden third factor can drive both, so they move together without one causing the other.

questions.prompt: Why do casinos profit in the long run?
choices: A small house edge repeated over millions of bets
They win every single hand
They only let unlucky people play
Luck always favors the house at night
questions.explanation: A tiny built-in edge per bet, multiplied across a mountain of bets, becomes reliable profit.

questions.prompt: The last 5 closing prices were $10, $12, $14, $16, and $18. What is the 5-day moving average, in dollars?
questions.explanation: ($10 + $12 + $14 + $16 + $18) / 5 = $70 / 5 = $14. Add the recent prices and divide by how many there are.

questions.prompt: Which are good risk-management habits? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Diversify across many investments
Risk only a small percent on any single trade
Put all your money in one hot stock
Size positions so a losing streak won't ruin you
questions.explanation: Spreading out, sizing small, and surviving losing streaks keep you in the game; betting everything on one pick does not.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Testing a strategy on past data
A smoothed line of recent prices
A built-in advantage for the casino
questions.explanation: These are the core ideas of the whole unit: test with data, smooth the noise, respect the edge, and spread your risk.

questions.prompt: Sort each into signal or noise.
items: A single odd tick that instantly reverses
questions.explanation: Signal is the real, lasting trend; noise is the random short-term jitter that a moving average smooths away.

questions.prompt: Order how a quant builds a strategy, first to last.
items: Form an idea about the market
Write it as a testable rule
Try it with a small real position
questions.explanation: Idea, rule, backtest, then a small live test: a disciplined loop that beats trading on a hunch.

questions.prompt: A 50% loss requires a 100% gain just to break even.
questions.explanation: Falling from $100 to $50 means you must double that $50 back to $100, a 100% gain, which is why avoiding big losses matters so much.
